question: For January 5–30, 2026, how many therapy sessions did Rowan attend, by service type and in total, and on how many distinct days? Provide a reviewable abstraction with source support and explain records that could lead to duplicate or ineligible counts.

statements.text: Rowan attended 12 therapy sessions (individual, group, and family psychotherapy) between January 5–30, 2026, across 11 distinct days: 5 individual sessions (January 5, 14, 19, 21, 26), 5 group sessions (January 6, 12, 19, 22, 29), and 2 family sessions (January 9, 30). Including the 2 medication management visits also attended in the period, the total of all attended visits is 14 across 12 distinct days.

Two medication management visits (January 13 with Elias Brenner NP, and January 30 with Elena Ortiz PMHNP) were attended but are not therapy and are excluded from the therapy session and day counts; they account for the difference between the 12 therapy sessions on 11 days and the 14 total attended visits on 12 days.

Several records require attention to avoid duplicate or ineligible counts: (1) The appointment desk export lists 9 encounters in one document — each is a separate visit counted once, not an additional session. (2) The outpatient attendance and disposition register lists 4 encounters (January 22, 27, 28, 29) in one document; each is counted once. (3) For the January 19 group session (HG-E110), four documents exist: the original roster, a copy retransmitted January 26 (no new information, not counted separately), a correction filed January 20 updating Rowan's departure time, and the group clinical record — all refer to the same single session. (4) The January 9 family session (HG-E104) has a co-facilitator addendum and a scheduling support log entry (a planned record, not an actual visit); both support the one counted session. (5) The scheduling support log also records an undated outbound phone call with no answer — no encounter number, not a therapy session, not counted. (6) A billing/administrative chart extract exists for the January 27 group no-show (HG-E116); that visit was not attended and is not counted, but the charge document could suggest a session occurred if reviewed in isolation. (7) January 19 has two counted therapy sessions — a group (HG-E110) and an individual (HG-E111) added because Rowan became anxious during group and needed individual grounding; both are legitimate distinct encounters. (8) January 30 has two attended visits — a family therapy session (HG-E119, counted) and a medication management visit (HG-E120, not counted as therapy). (9) The January 26 individual session (HG-E115) is documented by two clinicians whose notes give different start times (09:00 vs. 09:10) and different durations (50 vs. 40 minutes); attendance is agreed, so the session counts once, but the duration remains unresolved.

statements.why: Statement 0 provides concrete counts by service type (5 individual, 5 group, 2 family = 12 therapy sessions on 11 distinct days) and explains the difference between therapy sessions (12 on 11 days) and total attended visits (14 on 12 days) by identifying 2 medication management visits. All figures are supported by R2 (goal-eligible attended therapy encounters: 12 on 11 days, grouped by service type with specific dates and encounter IDs) and R3 (all attended encounters: 14 on 12 days). The individual session counts, dates, and clinician names are corroborated by the detailed encounter records in R2.1 (family: HG-E104 Jan 9, HG-E119 Jan 30), R2.2 (group: HG-E102 Jan 6, HG-E105 Jan 12, HG-E110 Jan 19, HG-E113 Jan 22, HG-E118 Jan 29), and R2.3 (individual: HG-E101 Jan 5, HG-E107 Jan 14, HG-E111 Jan 19, HG-E112 Jan 21, HG-E115 Jan 26). The medication management visits (HG-E106 Jan 13 with Elias Brenner NP, HG-E120 Jan 30 with Elena Ortiz PMHNP) are documented in R1.4 with disposition = excluded, confirming they are not therapy and account for the 2-visit difference.

Statement 1 correctly identifies the two medication management visits (HG-E106 on January 13 with Elias Brenner NP, and HG-E120 on January 30 with Elena Ortiz PMHNP) as attended but excluded from therapy counts. The evidence from R1.4 shows both encounters have delivered = yes and disposition = excluded, with service = medication. The statement accurately explains that these 2 visits account for the difference between 12 therapy sessions on 11 days and 14 total attended visits on 12 days. The dates, clinician names, and service type are all supported by the encounter records and facts provided.

Statement 2 comprehensively addresses duplicate and ineligible count risks with specific evidence: (1) Appointment desk export lists 9 encounters (R6.8: HG-E101–E109) as separate visits, each counted once—supported. (2) Outpatient attendance register lists 4 encounters (R6.7: HG-E113, HG-E116, HG-E117, HG-E118), each counted once—supported. (3) January 19 group (HG-E110) has four documents (R6.4, R6.5, R6.6: original roster, retransmitted copy, correction, clinical record) all referring to one session—supported by facts showing HG-E110 has records from BH-D101, BH-D102, BH-D103, BH-D104. (4) January 9 family (HG-E104) has co-facilitator addendum and scheduling log (R6.2, R6.3, R6.9)—supported; the addendum is noted in R2.1 as 'Accompanying clinical entry for the family appointment facilitated with Mara Voss (actual, addendum)'. (5) Undated phone call with no answer (R6.1, R6.9) is not a therapy session—supported by the unnumbered contact in the scheduling log. (6) January 27 group no-show (HG-E116) has billing/administrative record (R6.10) but was not attended—supported by R6.7 showing HG-E116 appointment_status = no_show. (7) January 19 has two legitimate distinct sessions (HG-E110 group, HG-E111 individual) with explanation of anxiety-driven individual grounding (R6.11)—supported by facts showing both encounters on 2026-01-19 with different services and clinicians. (8) January 30 has family therapy (HG-E119, counted) and medication management (HG-E120, not counted) (R6.12)—supported by facts showing both on 2026-01-30 with different services. (9) January 26 individual (HG-E115) has conflicting clinician notes on start time (09:00 vs. 09:10) and duration (50 vs. 40 minutes) but agreed attendance (R6.11, open items OI-1, OI-2, OI-3)—supported by facts showing HG-E115 has presence_start scenarios [09:00, 09:10], stated_minutes scenarios [50.0, 40.0], and minutes scenarios [40.0, 50.0], with status = conflicting.

populations.why: R1 counts 'all encounters in the review period where the patient attended (delivered = yes), of any service type, whether or not they count toward the care goal—including partial attendance and any excluded records.' This population is wider than the question asks. The question asks specifically for 'therapy sessions,' but R1 includes medication management visits (HG-E106, HG-E120) which are not therapy. The statement correctly uses R2 (goal-eligible attended therapy encounters only) for the therapy count, not R1.

R2 counts 'goal-eligible attended therapy encounters (disposition = included) in the review period—individual, group, and family psychotherapy only.' This matches the question's request for therapy sessions by service type. The population excludes medication management and other non-therapy services, and includes only attended (delivered = yes) encounters. The 12 therapy sessions on 11 distinct days from R2 directly answer the therapy-specific parts of the question.

R3 counts 'all attended (delivered = yes) encounters in the review period, across all service types.' This population is wider than the question asks for therapy sessions. R3 includes medication management visits (HG-E106, HG-E120) which are not therapy. The statement correctly uses R3 only to report the total of all attended visits (14 on 12 days) as supplementary context, not as the therapy session count.

R4 counts 'all goal-eligible attended therapy encounters (disposition = included) in the review period.' This matches the question's request for therapy sessions. R4 reports 12 encounters on 11 distinct days, which aligns with the therapy-specific answer. However, R4 does not break down by service type, so R2 (which does provide the breakdown) is the primary result used for the detailed answer.

R5 counts 'every encounter row in the review period, including not-attended, excluded, uncertain, and non-therapy service types.' This population is much wider than the question asks. R5 includes 20 encounters, of which 6 were not attended (cancelled, no-show, not present). The question asks only for attended therapy sessions, so R5 is not used for the primary answer; it is provided for context about excluded records.

R6 is a narrative result that 'records the count left out or that could change it' and documents every encounter and record in the period. It is not a count result and does not have a population in the sense of a specific numeric query. It is used to support the explanation of duplicate and ineligible count risks, not to provide a count itself.

question: How many therapy minutes and hours did Rowan actually receive during the review period, overall and for each Monday–Sunday week? Show calculations or supporting detail, and report any conclusion the available documents do not settle.

statements.text: Across the full review period (January 5–30, 2026), Rowan received therapy in 12 sessions on 11 days, totalling either 585 or 595 minutes (9 hours 45 minutes or 9 hours 55 minutes) — the exact total cannot be settled because of a conflict in one session (see below).

By Monday–Sunday week: Week 1 (Jan 5–11): 3 sessions — individual Jan 5 (50 min), group Jan 6 (45 min), family Jan 9 (45 min) — total 140 minutes (2 h 20 min). Week 2 (Jan 12–18): 2 sessions — group Jan 12 (75 min), individual Jan 14 (45 min) — total 120 minutes (2 h 0 min). Week 3 (Jan 19–25): 4 sessions — group Jan 19 (60 min), individual Jan 19 (30 min), individual Jan 21 (45 min), group Jan 22 (45 min) — total 180 minutes (3 h 0 min). Week 4 (Jan 26–30, partial week): 3 sessions — individual Jan 26 (40 or 50 min), group Jan 29 (75 min), family Jan 30 (30 min) — total 145 or 155 minutes (2 h 25 min or 2 h 35 min).

question: Summarize the documented symptom course during the episode and the reason for the additional individual contact on January 19. Which symptom assessments are distinct, and what conclusions about progress can and cannot be supported?

statements.text: At intake (January 5), Rowan presented with several weeks of low mood, reduced interest in activities, fragmented sleep with repeated night waking, difficulty beginning tasks, and work-related anxiety driving avoidance of emails and conversations about a return date. Through the first two weeks these symptoms persisted largely unchanged: sleep remained interrupted, mornings were difficult, and avoidance of work communication continued, though Rowan noted mood felt somewhat less heavy on days with a planned activity (January 13). By mid-episode (January 14–16) the clinician observed affect more varied than at intake, and a clinician review noted some improvement in depressive symptoms while avoidance and inconsistent sleep continued. On January 19 Rowan became visibly tense and overwhelmed during group discussion of workplace demands. In the final week, Rowan sent a message to the supervisor (January 26) but continued to postpone scheduling the follow-up conversation; sleep remained uneven, tied to repetitive work-related thoughts at night. By January 30 Rowan reported mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month, though anxiety about work contact remained noticeable and sleep was still variable.

The individual contact on January 19 (encounter HG-E111, 11:15–11:45, with Mira Patel, LCSW) was an unscheduled, same-day addition. It was arranged because Rowan became acutely anxious during the skills group when discussion turned to returning to the workplace, said the amount of discussion felt difficult to manage, and requested additional help. The group facilitator offered grounding and arranged the individual meeting; Rowan came directly from the group room.

Three distinct PHQ-9 total scores were recorded during the episode: 18 on January 5, 14 on January 16, and 10 on January 30. These are the only three administrations; no other PHQ-9 total scores were recorded in this period.

Progress that can be supported: The PHQ-9 total fell from 18 at intake to 10 at episode end, a change of −8 points (−44.4%). Clinician observations corroborate a directional shift: affect was described as more varied than at intake by January 14, and both the patient and the treating clinician noted fewer days of pervasive low mood by January 30. Rowan also completed a concrete behavioral step—sending a message to the supervisor—that had not occurred earlier in the episode.

Progress that cannot be supported: Sleep disruption was present at intake and remained variable and clinically relevant at episode end, with no documented sustained improvement. Work-related anxiety and avoidance also persisted throughout: Rowan continued to postpone scheduling the follow-up conversation with the supervisor as of January 26–30, and the clinician noted persistent avoidance with meaningful functional impact at episode end. The record contains no standardized anxiety measure and no objective sleep data, so the degree of change in these domains cannot be quantified.

statements.text: At intake (January 5), Rowan presented with several weeks of low mood, reduced interest in activities, fragmented sleep with repeated night waking, difficulty beginning tasks, and work-related anxiety driving avoidance of emails and conversations about a return date. Through the first two weeks these symptoms persisted largely unchanged: sleep remained interrupted, mornings were difficult, and avoidance of work communication continued, though Rowan noted mood felt somewhat less heavy on days with a planned activity (January 13). By mid-episode (January 14–16) the clinician observed affect more varied than at intake, and a clinician review noted some improvement in depressive symptoms while avoidance and inconsistent sleep continued. On January 19 Rowan became visibly tense and overwhelmed during group discussion of workplace demands. In the final week, Rowan sent a message to the supervisor (January 26) but continued to postpone scheduling the follow-up conversation; sleep remained uneven, tied to repetitive work-related thoughts at night. By January 30 Rowan reported mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month, though anxiety about work contact remained noticeable and sleep was still variable.

The individual contact on January 19 (encounter HG-E111, 11:15–11:45, with Mira Patel, LCSW) was an unscheduled, same-day addition. It was arranged because Rowan became acutely anxious during the skills group when discussion turned to returning to the workplace, said the amount of discussion felt difficult to manage, and requested additional help. The group facilitator offered grounding and arranged the individual meeting; Rowan came directly from the group room.

Three distinct PHQ-9 total scores were recorded during the episode: 18 on January 5, 14 on January 16, and 10 on January 30. These are the only three administrations; no other PHQ-9 total scores were recorded in this period.

Progress that can be supported: The PHQ-9 total fell from 18 at intake to 10 at episode end, a change of −8 points (−44.4%). Clinician observations corroborate a directional shift: affect was described as more varied than at intake by January 14, and both the patient and the treating clinician noted fewer days of pervasive low mood by January 30. Rowan also completed a concrete behavioral step—sending a message to the supervisor—that had not occurred earlier in the episode.

Progress that cannot be supported: Sleep disruption was present at intake and remained variable and clinically relevant at episode end, with no documented sustained improvement. Work-related anxiety and avoidance also persisted throughout: Rowan continued to postpone scheduling the follow-up conversation with the supervisor as of January 26–30, and the clinician noted persistent avoidance with meaningful functional impact at episode end. The record contains no standardized anxiety measure and no objective sleep data, so the degree of change in these domains cannot be quantified.

question: By January 30, what evidence supports improvement and what evidence limits a conclusion of recovery? Integrate symptoms with functioning.

statements.text: Evidence supporting improvement: The PHQ-9 fell from 18 on January 5 to 14 on January 16 and to 10 on January 30, a trajectory the clinician described as partial improvement. Rowan's own report on January 30 was that mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month, with fewer days of pervasive low mood than at intake. Functionally, Rowan completed small activities by January 14 (opening a work message, short walks), and by January 26 had sent a message to the supervisor and received a reply — a concrete step not present at intake. Affect was noted to be more varied than at intake by January 14. Casey confirmed Rowan was getting out for walks and seemed more willing to discuss the coming week by January 16, and the scheduled evening check-in had reduced unplanned reminders. On January 30 Rowan was alert, organized in conversation, and able to describe the follow-up plan, and reported that having a limited plan felt more manageable.

Evidence limiting a conclusion of recovery: Despite the PHQ-9 decline, a score of 10 on January 30 remains in the mild-to-moderate range, and the clinician explicitly characterized the picture as partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work. Avoidance of work communication was unresolved throughout: Rowan had not replied to the original work message as of January 14, drafted but did not send a message until around January 26, and as of January 29–30 was still delaying the follow-up conversation with the supervisor after receiving a reply. Sleep disruption persisted across every week of the period — described as interrupted, inconsistent, or variable on January 5, 13, 14, 16, 21, 26, and 30 — and the clinician noted it remained an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine. Anxiety remained noticeable when anticipating work contact on January 30 (patient and clinician reports), and Rowan became visibly tense during group discussion of workplace return on January 19, requiring a same-day individual session. The pattern of reminders triggering withdrawal was still active on January 30, and Rowan continued to delay scheduling the supervisor conversation even after the message was sent.

omitted.text: The Harbor Grove Behavioral Health administrative import receipt is a copy of a document that originated at the treating site: it reproduces the January 16 PHQ-9 score of 14 and the clinician's review note (Mara Voss, LCSW, timestamped January 16, 2026, 09:10) but adds no independent clinician signature and records no additional visit. Because it is a copy rather than an independent source, it does not corroborate the January 16 PHQ-9 score on its own; the score is instead supported by the original symptom measure review document from January 16. The copy's presence means the January 16 PHQ-9 of 14 is documented but not corroborated by two independent sources, which is why its status differs from the January 5 score of 18 (which is corroborated by two independent documents).

statements.text: Evidence supporting improvement: The PHQ-9 fell from 18 on January 5 to 14 on January 16 and to 10 on January 30, a trajectory the clinician described as partial improvement. Rowan's own report on January 30 was that mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month, with fewer days of pervasive low mood than at intake. Functionally, Rowan completed small activities by January 14 (opening a work message, short walks), and by January 26 had sent a message to the supervisor and received a reply — a concrete step not present at intake. Affect was noted to be more varied than at intake by January 14. Casey confirmed Rowan was getting out for walks and seemed more willing to discuss the coming week by January 16, and the scheduled evening check-in had reduced unplanned reminders. On January 30 Rowan was alert, organized in conversation, and able to describe the follow-up plan, and reported that having a limited plan felt more manageable.

Evidence limiting a conclusion of recovery: Despite the PHQ-9 decline, a score of 10 on January 30 remains in the mild-to-moderate range, and the clinician explicitly characterized the picture as partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work. Avoidance of work communication was unresolved throughout: Rowan had not replied to the original work message as of January 14, drafted but did not send a message until around January 26, and as of January 29–30 was still delaying the follow-up conversation with the supervisor after receiving a reply. Sleep disruption persisted across every week of the period — described as interrupted, inconsistent, or variable on January 5, 13, 14, 16, 21, 26, and 30 — and the clinician noted it remained an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine. Anxiety remained noticeable when anticipating work contact on January 30 (patient and clinician reports), and Rowan became visibly tense during group discussion of workplace return on January 19, requiring a same-day individual session. The pattern of reminders triggering withdrawal was still active on January 30, and Rowan continued to delay scheduling the supervisor conversation even after the message was sent.

The Harbor Grove Behavioral Health administrative import receipt is a copy of a document that originated at the treating site: it reproduces the January 16 PHQ-9 score of 14 and the clinician's review note (Mara Voss, LCSW, timestamped January 16, 2026, 09:10) but adds no independent clinician signature and records no additional visit. Because it is a copy rather than an independent source, it does not corroborate the January 16 PHQ-9 score on its own; the score is instead supported by the original symptom measure review document from January 16. The copy's presence means the January 16 PHQ-9 of 14 is documented but not corroborated by two independent sources, which is why its status differs from the January 5 score of 18 (which is corroborated by two independent documents).

question: Trace Rowan’s work-communication progress from early January through January 30. Distinguish a planned action, drafting, sending, and completed follow-up.

statements.text: Planned actions: From January 5, the treatment plan set out that individual sessions would address avoided communication and gradual preparation for return to employment, and that the team would combine individual, group, and family work. Rowan expressed wanting a manageable work-transition routine. On January 9, Casey agreed to a single planned check-in about work preparation rather than repeated reminders. On January 13, Rowan was directed to bring activity and communication concerns to the treating therapist. On January 19, the plan after the individual crisis visit was to review how the smaller task went at the next visit. On January 23, the outside social worker was to provide contact information and help organize documents if requested. On January 26, the plan included maintaining scheduled treatment contact during the return-to-work period and bringing the response draft to the next visit if Rowan remained stuck. On January 30, the plan was to continue the current outpatient treatment and revisit whether the agreed communication pattern had been useful.

Drafting activity: On January 14, a session focused on separating a brief acknowledgment from a commitment to a work schedule; a short response was drafted in Rowan's own words and practiced aloud. On January 19, the task was narrowed to drafting two sentences to a supervisor without requiring the message be sent that day, and Rowan was encouraged to allow an incomplete draft to exist rather than abandon it over imperfect wording. By January 21, Rowan reported having drafted a short message about a possible gradual return to work but stopping before sending it; the session then practiced reading the draft once and choosing a planned time to send it. Rowan also identified repeatedly checking the draft as a further way of delaying the task.

Sending activity: By January 26, Rowan reported having sent a short message to the supervisor and receiving a reply asking to discuss possible next steps. The January 26 session rehearsed a brief response to that reply, with Rowan's partner Nora Ellis helping rehearse a grounding cue to use before sending it. The record does not document whether that follow-on response was actually sent after the session.

Completed follow-up: On January 14, Rowan reported completing several small activities since the prior individual appointment, including opening a work message. The supervisor's reply to Rowan's sent message (received before January 26) constitutes the one documented external response: it reduced one uncertainty but raised worry about being asked for commitments Rowan might not be able to meet. By January 29, Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying the follow-up conversation with the supervisor. The January 30 clinician review noted that Rowan had taken initial steps including drafting and sending a message, but continued to delay follow-up and became anxious when a task expanded beyond a narrowly defined action.

Reason for care: Rowan describes several weeks of low mood, reduced interest in usual activities, fragmented sleep, and difficulty beginning ordinary tasks. Worry increases when thinking about returning to work after a recent leave. Rowan has been postponing email replies, avoiding conversations about the return date, and spending more time alone at home. They want a routine that makes the work transition feel manageable. The current outpatient episode is planned for January 5 through January 30, with review as treatment progresses.

This visit was added because Rowan became anxious during group and needed individual grounding and review of coping strategies. Rowan came directly from the group room. The patient described feeling overwhelmed when other members discussed workplace demands and worried that returning to work would expose difficulties keeping up. Rowan was able to identify muscle tension, rapid breathing, and an urge to leave as early signs of activation.

Rowan described sending a short message to the supervisor and receiving a request to discuss possible next steps. The reply reduced one uncertainty but also brought up worry about being asked for commitments the patient might not be able to meet. Rowan continued to postpone choosing a time for the conversation. Sleep remained uneven, with difficulty settling on nights when work-related thoughts became repetitive.

statements.text: Planned actions: From January 5, the treatment plan set out that individual sessions would address avoided communication and gradual preparation for return to employment, and that the team would combine individual, group, and family work. Rowan expressed wanting a manageable work-transition routine. On January 9, Casey agreed to a single planned check-in about work preparation rather than repeated reminders. On January 13, Rowan was directed to bring activity and communication concerns to the treating therapist. On January 19, the plan after the individual crisis visit was to review how the smaller task went at the next visit. On January 23, the outside social worker was to provide contact information and help organize documents if requested. On January 26, the plan included maintaining scheduled treatment contact during the return-to-work period and bringing the response draft to the next visit if Rowan remained stuck. On January 30, the plan was to continue the current outpatient treatment and revisit whether the agreed communication pattern had been useful.

Drafting activity: On January 14, a session focused on separating a brief acknowledgment from a commitment to a work schedule; a short response was drafted in Rowan's own words and practiced aloud. On January 19, the task was narrowed to drafting two sentences to a supervisor without requiring the message be sent that day, and Rowan was encouraged to allow an incomplete draft to exist rather than abandon it over imperfect wording. By January 21, Rowan reported having drafted a short message about a possible gradual return to work but stopping before sending it; the session then practiced reading the draft once and choosing a planned time to send it. Rowan also identified repeatedly checking the draft as a further way of delaying the task.

Sending activity: By January 26, Rowan reported having sent a short message to the supervisor and receiving a reply asking to discuss possible next steps. The January 26 session rehearsed a brief response to that reply, with Rowan's partner Nora Ellis helping rehearse a grounding cue to use before sending it. The record does not document whether that follow-on response was actually sent after the session.

Completed follow-up: On January 14, Rowan reported completing several small activities since the prior individual appointment, including opening a work message. The supervisor's reply to Rowan's sent message (received before January 26) constitutes the one documented external response: it reduced one uncertainty but raised worry about being asked for commitments Rowan might not be able to meet. By January 29, Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying the follow-up conversation with the supervisor. The January 30 clinician review noted that Rowan had taken initial steps including drafting and sending a message, but continued to delay follow-up and became anxious when a task expanded beyond a narrowly defined action.

question: Identify the recurring psychotherapy strategies used for avoidance and task initiation, with examples from different dates. What evidence distinguishes rehearsal from independent follow-through?

statements.text: Two recurring strategies address avoidance: (1) psychoeducation about the anxiety–avoidance cycle — mapping the sequence from triggering situation → anxious prediction → physical activation → avoidance response (January 5, developing a shared description of the sleep/worry/avoidance cycle; January 19 group, worked example using an unanswered work email); and (2) behavioral activation / approach behavior selection — identifying and committing to a small, observable approach step rather than withdrawing (January 5, breaking one work task into a short observable step; January 19 group, members selected a small approach behavior to attempt during the week; January 22 group, translating a broad intention into one action completable in a few minutes).

Two recurring strategies address task initiation: (1) task decomposition — breaking a complicated task into the smallest observable first step and identifying the cue that would prompt it (January 5, practicing breaking one work task into a short observable step; January 14, narrowing the work task to drafting two sentences without requiring the message be sent; January 19 individual, narrowing to drafting two sentences and allowing an incomplete draft to exist; January 22 group, reducing a task to an action completable in a few minutes with a named cue; January 23 coordination review, helping Rowan break a difficult task into a manageable first step); and (2) in-session rehearsal of the specific action — practicing the wording, timing, or communication step aloud before attempting it independently (January 6, practicing breaking a task into a step; January 14, drafting a short response in Rowan's own words and practicing it aloud; January 21, practicing reading the draft once and choosing a planned send time; January 26, role-play of a brief response to the supervisor; January 26, rehearsing requesting a brief initial conversation with a specific purpose; January 30, rehearsing requesting a specific kind of help from Casey).

The clearest distinction between rehearsal and independent follow-through is documented on January 26: Rowan could use the grounding cue during the in-session rehearsal but remained uncertain about using it independently when anxious, and the clinician noted the patient was hesitant about completing the task outside the office. This directly contrasts structured, clinician-supported practice (rehearsal) with self-initiated use under real anxiety (independent follow-through). The pattern across the record reinforces this: rehearsal produced engagement and partial skill use with prompting, while between-session reports consistently showed partial completion — approach steps started but not carried through to the next stage.

Rehearsal is documented as clinician-facilitated, in-session practice: January 6, the facilitator demonstrated paced breathing and invited short practice rounds; January 9, Rowan practiced asking for one specific kind of help while Casey practiced reflecting the request, with a communication rehearsal guided by the clinician; January 14, a short response was drafted and practiced aloud in session; January 21, Rowan practiced reading the draft once and choosing a planned send time; January 26, clinicians used role-play to identify when Rowan shifted from asking a question into apologizing, and a grounding cue was rehearsed before sending; January 29, Rowan participated in a paired rehearsal and accepted feedback about keeping the request brief; January 30, a rehearsal was facilitated in which Casey asked what kind of support Rowan wanted and Rowan practiced naming when a reminder felt overwhelming.

Independent follow-through — applying skills between sessions without clinician support — is documented through patient self-report at subsequent visits: January 9, Rowan said an evening walk felt more acceptable than reviewing unfinished tasks (approach behavior attempted outside session); January 21, Rowan reported having drafted a short message about a gradual return to work but stopping before sending it; January 26, Rowan reported sending the message to the supervisor and receiving a reply, but continued to postpone choosing a time for the follow-up conversation; January 29, Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying a follow-up conversation. Clinician review, January 30: Rowan shows partial improvement, with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work. The patient has taken some initial steps, including drafting and sending a message, but continues to delay follow-up and becomes anxious when a task expands beyond a narrowly defined action. This visit was added because Rowan became anxious during group and needed individual grounding and review of coping strategies. Rowan came directly from the group room. The patient described feeling overwhelmed when other members discussed workplace demands and worried that returning to work would expose difficulties keeping up. Rowan was able to identify muscle tension, rapid breathing, and an urge to leave as early signs of activation.

Group focus: recognizing early physical signs of anxiety and choosing a coping response before withdrawing from a task. statements.text: Two recurring strategies address avoidance: (1) psychoeducation about the anxiety–avoidance cycle — mapping the sequence from triggering situation → anxious prediction → physical activation → avoidance response (January 5, developing a shared description of the sleep/worry/avoidance cycle; January 19 group, worked example using an unanswered work email); and (2) behavioral activation / approach behavior selection — identifying and committing to a small, observable approach step rather than withdrawing (January 5, breaking one work task into a short observable step; January 19 group, members selected a small approach behavior to attempt during the week; January 22 group, translating a broad intention into one action completable in a few minutes).

Two recurring strategies address task initiation: (1) task decomposition — breaking a complicated task into the smallest observable first step and identifying the cue that would prompt it (January 5, practicing breaking one work task into a short observable step; January 14, narrowing the work task to drafting two sentences without requiring the message be sent; January 19 individual, narrowing to drafting two sentences and allowing an incomplete draft to exist; January 22 group, reducing a task to an action completable in a few minutes with a named cue; January 23 coordination review, helping Rowan break a difficult task into a manageable first step); and (2) in-session rehearsal of the specific action — practicing the wording, timing, or communication step aloud before attempting it independently (January 6, practicing breaking a task into a step; January 14, drafting a short response in Rowan's own words and practicing it aloud; January 21, practicing reading the draft once and choosing a planned send time; January 26, role-play of a brief response to the supervisor; January 26, rehearsing requesting a brief initial conversation with a specific purpose; January 30, rehearsing requesting a specific kind of help from Casey).

Rehearsal is documented as clinician-facilitated, in-session practice: January 6, the facilitator demonstrated paced breathing and invited short practice rounds; January 9, Rowan practiced asking for one specific kind of help while Casey practiced reflecting the request, with a communication rehearsal guided by the clinician; January 14, a short response was drafted and practiced aloud in session; January 21, Rowan practiced reading the draft once and choosing a planned send time; January 26, clinicians used role-play to identify when Rowan shifted from asking a question into apologizing, and a grounding cue was rehearsed before sending; January 29, Rowan participated in a paired rehearsal and accepted feedback about keeping the request brief; January 30, a rehearsal was facilitated in which Casey asked what kind of support Rowan wanted and Rowan practiced naming when a reminder felt overwhelming.

Independent follow-through — applying skills between sessions without clinician support — is documented through patient self-report at subsequent visits: January 9, Rowan said an evening walk felt more acceptable than reviewing unfinished tasks (approach behavior attempted outside session); January 21, Rowan reported having drafted a short message about a gradual return to work but stopping before sending it; January 26, Rowan reported sending the message to the supervisor and receiving a reply, but continued to postpone choosing a time for the follow-up conversation; January 29, Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying a follow-up conversation. A January 30 clinician review noted that Rowan had taken some initial steps including drafting and sending a message, but continued to delay follow-up.

The clearest distinction between rehearsal and independent follow-through is documented on January 26: Rowan could use the grounding cue during the in-session rehearsal but remained uncertain about using it independently when anxious, and the clinician noted the patient was hesitant about completing the task outside the office. This directly contrasts structured, clinician-supported practice (rehearsal) with self-initiated use under real anxiety (independent follow-through). The pattern across the record reinforces this: rehearsal produced engagement and partial skill use with prompting, while between-session reports consistently showed partial completion — approach steps started but not carried through to the next stage.

question: Summarize the course of sleep difficulty during the episode. Does the record support saying that sleep normalized by the final week?

statements.text: Sleep difficulty was present throughout the episode and never fully resolved. At intake (January 5), Rowan described several weeks of fragmented sleep, and the clinician listed sleep disruption as a presenting need. On January 8, a poor night of sleep caused Rowan to miss an appointment. Sleep interruption and daytime tiredness continued through January 13–14. By January 16, the clinician noted some improvement in depressive symptoms but described sleep as still inconsistent and clinically relevant. On January 19, disrupted sleep continued to interfere with resuming a work routine. On January 21, Rowan reported one improved night followed by a night of prolonged wakefulness. On January 26, sleep remained uneven, tied to repetitive work-related thoughts at night. At the episode's close on January 30, Rowan still endorsed sleep difficulty, described sleep as variable, and the clinician noted sleep disruption as an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine.

The record does not support saying sleep normalized by the final week. In the last week (January 26–30), both the patient and the clinician consistently described sleep as uneven, variable, and an ongoing barrier. The plan on January 30 was to continue monitoring sleep, not to note resolution. The only positive change noted by episode end was fewer days of pervasive low mood, not improvement in sleep.

passages.text: Assessment: ongoing depressive and anxiety symptoms with sleep disruption. Rowan is engaged with the therapy program and intends to continue the scheduled appointments. Medication monitoring will continue during the outpatient episode, with later follow-up arranged according to clinical response.
Review: assess participation, symptoms, and practical functioning during the episode. Adjust the schedule when clinically indicated or when access barriers arise.

Reason for care: Rowan describes several weeks of low mood, reduced interest in usual activities, fragmented sleep, and difficulty beginning ordinary tasks. Worry increases when thinking about returning to work after a recent leave. Rowan has been postponing email replies, avoiding conversations about the return date, and spending more time alone at home. They want a routine that makes the work transition feel manageable. The current outpatient episode is planned for January 5 through January 30, with review as treatment progresses.

Clinician review: the score and recent individual-session material suggest some improvement in depressive symptoms. Persistent avoidance, difficulty initiating work communication, and sleep disruption remain clinically relevant. Rowan has attempted small activities and communication practice but has not yet established a reliable routine. Continue the current therapeutic focus and review functioning alongside symptom change during the next direct appointment.

Rowan completed the questionnaire before the afternoon appointment. The patient continued to endorse sleep difficulty and trouble sustaining usual activities, with fewer days of pervasive low mood than reported at intake. The form was available to the treating clinician for review with the patient's account of functioning.

Today's group addressed recognizing the sequence between a triggering situation, an anxious prediction, physical activation, and an avoidance response. The facilitator used a worked example involving an unanswered work email. Members then practiced describing the prediction without treating it as an established outcome, and selected a small approach behavior they could attempt during the week. The break was for restroom use and refreshments; there was no facilitated discussion, assigned therapeutic activity, or patient treatment during that interval.

We mapped a recent morning interaction and paused at points where each person made assumptions. Rowan practiced asking for one specific kind of help, and Casey practiced reflecting the request before offering suggestions. Leena Park guided a short communication rehearsal while I observed and helped the pair identify language they could use during the next week.
The batch received this morning contains the following measurement summary for the outpatient episode. The source record identifies the patient portal submission retained by the treatment team.

statements.text: Sleep difficulty was present throughout the episode and never fully resolved. At intake (January 5), Rowan described several weeks of fragmented sleep, and the clinician listed sleep disruption as a presenting need. On January 8, a poor night of sleep caused Rowan to miss an appointment. Sleep interruption and daytime tiredness continued through January 13–14. By January 16, the clinician noted some improvement in depressive symptoms but described sleep as still inconsistent and clinically relevant. On January 19, disrupted sleep continued to interfere with resuming a work routine. On January 21, Rowan reported one improved night followed by a night of prolonged wakefulness. On January 26, sleep remained uneven, tied to repetitive work-related thoughts at night. At the episode's close on January 30, Rowan still endorsed sleep difficulty, described sleep as variable, and the clinician noted sleep disruption as an intermittent barrier to a steadier daytime routine.

The record does not support saying sleep normalized by the final week. In the last week (January 26–30), both the patient and the clinician consistently described sleep as uneven, variable, and an ongoing barrier. The plan on January 30 was to continue monitoring sleep, not to note resolution. The only positive change noted by episode end was fewer days of pervasive low mood, not improvement in sleep.

statements.why: The narrative provides a comprehensive chronological summary of sleep difficulty from intake through episode close. Each date-specific claim is supported by cited evidence: fragmented sleep at intake (FIN:O-5c787ca0), poor sleep on January 8 (FIN:O-415a1958), continuing sleep interruption on January 13-14 (FIN:O-cc98cbe2, FIN:O-76b728e7), inconsistent sleep on January 16 (FIN:O-18ea4787, FIN:O-dc6a5969), disrupted sleep on January 19 (FIN:O-030db061), mixed sleep on January 21 (FIN:O-fa912dc5), uneven sleep on January 26 (FIN:O-07fc9b63), and variable sleep at episode close on January 30 (FIN:O-a2a580a6, FIN:O-3be7d99f). The conclusion that sleep 'never fully resolved' is supported by the consistent presence of sleep difficulty throughout and the final clinician note that sleep disruption 'remains an intermittent barrier' (FIN:O-5d13b4ae).

The statement correctly identifies that the record does not support sleep normalization by the final week. Evidence from the final week (January 26-30) consistently describes sleep as uneven (FIN:O-07fc9b63), variable (FIN:O-a2a580a6), and an ongoing barrier (FIN:O-5d13b4ae). The patient continued to endorse sleep difficulty at episode close (FIN:O-3be7d99f). The plan on January 30 was to 'monitor sleep' (FIN:O-dfeafb17), indicating ongoing concern rather than resolution. The statement accurately notes that the only positive change was fewer days of pervasive low mood, not sleep improvement, which is supported by FIN:O-3be7d99f.

question: Which January 16 observations came from Casey, and which came from Rowan’s own questionnaire update? Why does that distinction matter?

statements.text: Casey's observations came from the collateral contact (encounter HG-E109), a session with Mara Voss, LCSW and Casey Mercer alone — Rowan was not present. Casey reported four things: that Rowan had been getting out for short walks and seemed more willing to discuss the coming week; that mornings remain difficult and Rowan becomes quiet when conversation turns to work; that the scheduled evening check-in has reduced unplanned reminders; and that it takes effort to resist offering multiple solutions, but there is less argument when Casey asks what kind of help Rowan wants.

Rowan's own questionnaire update — a PHQ-9 submitted through the patient portal on January 16 at 08:17, with an optional free-text field — contributed three findings in Rowan's own words: getting out of the apartment had become a little easier; thinking about work continued to make them want to put things off; and sleep was inconsistent.

The distinction matters because the two sources carry different clinical weight. Casey's account reflects an outside observer's perspective on Rowan's behavior at home — useful for tracking functioning but filtered through Casey's interpretation. Rowan's own questionnaire responses reflect Rowan's subjective experience directly. Where they overlap (e.g., both sources note sleep difficulty and avoidance of work topics), the agreement strengthens confidence in those findings. Where they differ in emphasis — Casey noted improved willingness to discuss the coming week, while Rowan's own words focused on ongoing avoidance — the clinician noted that Casey's information would be incorporated only at the next direct appointment with Rowan, and that no treatment decision was made on the basis of the collateral contact alone.

Casey reported four things: that Rowan had been getting out for short walks and seemed more willing to discuss the coming week; that mornings remain difficult and Rowan becomes quiet when conversation turns to work; that the scheduled evening check-in has reduced unplanned reminders; and that it takes effort to resist offering multiple solutions, but there is less argument when Casey asks what kind of help Rowan wants.

Rowan's own questionnaire update — a PHQ-9 submitted through the patient portal on January 16 at 08:17, with an optional free-text field — contributed three findings in Rowan's own words: getting out of the apartment had become a little easier; thinking about work continued to make them want to put things off; and sleep was inconsistent.

The distinction matters because the two sources carry different clinical weight. Casey's account reflects an outside observer's perspective on Rowan's behavior at home — useful for tracking functioning but filtered through Casey's interpretation. Rowan's own questionnaire responses reflect Rowan's subjective experience directly. Where they overlap (e.g., both sources note sleep difficulty and avoidance of work topics), the agreement strengthens confidence in those findings. Where they differ in emphasis — Casey noted improved willingness to discuss the coming week, while Rowan's own words focused on ongoing avoidance — the clinician noted that Casey's information would be incorporated only at the next direct appointment with Rowan, and that no treatment decision was made on the basis of the collateral contact alone.

question: What family communication plan was developed on January 9, and how was that theme revisited on January 30? Does the later note prove the issue was already resolved?

statements.text: On January 9, the family session (with Rowan, Casey, Mara Voss LCSW, and Leena Park LPC) produced a three-part communication plan: (1) Casey agreed to replace repeated reminders with a single planned check-in about work preparation; (2) Rowan agreed to say when they wanted practical help versus quiet company; and (3) the couple chose a shared evening walk as a pressure-free activity. Clinicians used reflective listening exercises and a communication rehearsal to help both partners understand how their intentions differed from how the other experienced them.

On January 30, the family session (encounter HG-E119, with Mira Patel LCSW) revisited the same theme: Rowan and Casey identified that the pattern of reminders about contacting work was still leading to lengthy discussions followed by Rowan withdrawing from the task, and Casey still described uncertainty about when reminders helped versus increased pressure. The clinician ran another communication rehearsal — Casey practiced asking what kind of support Rowan wanted, and Rowan practiced naming when a reminder felt overwhelming. Both then agreed again to try one brief, planned check-in rather than repeated questions across the evening. The plan noted that whether the agreed communication pattern had been useful would need to be revisited at a future visit.

The January 30 note does not prove the issue was already resolved. On the contrary, it documents the same recurring pattern still present — reminders continuing to trigger withdrawal — and the plan explicitly defers judgment on whether the agreed communication approach was working. Rowan remained anxious about the work conversation, and the clinician's overall assessment was partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact.

question: Which formal psychiatric diagnosis and diagnostic code are established by these documents? Distinguish clinical symptom descriptions from a coded diagnosis.

statements.text: No formal coded psychiatric diagnosis (such as an ICD-10 or DSM-5 code) is recorded anywhere in these documents. The record does not contain a diagnosis field, a diagnostic code, or a named disorder assigned by a clinician.

The closest the documents come to a diagnostic impression is the clinician's characterization at intake: "depressive symptoms with anxiety and behavioral avoidance." A later assessment entry reads "ongoing depressive and anxiety symptoms with sleep disruption." These are clinical impression statements, not a coded diagnosis. A formal diagnosis with an ICD or DSM code, entered in a diagnosis field and signed by a treating clinician, would be needed to establish a coded disorder.

The clinical symptom descriptions documented across the record, distinct from any coded diagnosis, include: low mood and reduced interest in usual activities for several weeks; fragmented and interrupted sleep with daytime fatigue; difficulty beginning ordinary tasks; worry and anxiety about returning to work; avoidance of work communication (delaying email replies, not sending drafted messages, postponing scheduling a conversation with a supervisor); behavioral avoidance that worsens with discussion of workplace demands; muscle tension, rapid breathing, and an urge to leave as physical signs of anxiety; repetitive planning at night interfering with sleep; and a pattern of withdrawing from tasks after reminders about work.

statements.text: No formal coded psychiatric diagnosis (such as an ICD-10 or DSM-5 code) is recorded anywhere in these documents. The record does not contain a diagnosis field, a diagnostic code, or a named disorder assigned by a clinician.

The closest the documents come to a diagnostic impression is the clinician's characterization at intake: "depressive symptoms with anxiety and behavioral avoidance." A later assessment entry reads "ongoing depressive and anxiety symptoms with sleep disruption." These are clinical impression statements, not a coded diagnosis. A formal diagnosis with an ICD or DSM code, entered in a diagnosis field and signed by a treating clinician, would be needed to establish a coded disorder.

The clinical symptom descriptions documented across the record, distinct from any coded diagnosis, include: low mood and reduced interest in usual activities for several weeks; fragmented and interrupted sleep with daytime fatigue; difficulty beginning ordinary tasks; worry and anxiety about returning to work; avoidance of work communication (delaying email replies, not sending drafted messages, postponing scheduling a conversation with a supervisor); behavioral avoidance that worsens with discussion of workplace demands; muscle tension, rapid breathing, and an urge to leave as physical signs of anxiety; repetitive planning at night interfering with sleep; and a pattern of withdrawing from tasks after reminders about work.

question: On what date did Rowan return to work, and what work schedule or employment clearance had been approved by the end of the episode?

statements.text: The record does not document a date on which Rowan returned to work. Throughout the episode (January 5–30, 2026), Rowan had not yet returned; notes consistently describe ongoing avoidance of work communication, anxiety about reconnecting with work, and persistent functional difficulty around work demands.

No work schedule or employment clearance was approved by the end of the episode. As of January 23, an outside social worker reported that Rowan had asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return schedule, and the professionals clarified that neither of them made an employment determination during that call. The end-of-episode clinician review on January 30 noted partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work, and recommended continued treatment.

rows().subject: FIN:O-b117f3fb
rows().value: Casey reflected Rowan's wish to keep ownership of the return-to-work process.

rows().subject: FIN:O-669013b6
rows().value: Casey agreed to use a single planned check-in about work preparation instead of repeated reminders.

rows().subject: FIN:O-306e7fff
rows().value: Rowan described feeling watched when asked repeatedly whether they had contacted work.

rows().subject: FIN:O-19450fb6
rows().value: Rowan contributed an example about leaving work messages unopened and identified looking at one message as a lower step than replying to every outstanding message.

rows().subject: FIN:O-f7accf3e
rows().value: No separate psychotherapy component was provided or documented. Rowan was directed to bring activity and communication concerns to the treating therapist for continued work.

rows().subject: FIN:O-39cf04c7
rows().value: Rowan described mood as somewhat less heavy on days with a planned activity but remained concerned about work communication.

rows().subject: FIN:O-06af2ed4
rows().value: Rowan noticed physical tension during the rehearsal but was able to remain with the task; they said the message seemed less overwhelming when it did not need to solve the entire return-to-work question.

rows().subject: FIN:O-cbc32346
rows().value: Rowan has not yet replied to the work message and continues to imagine being asked questions they cannot answer.

rows().subject: FIN:O-1a32e8ec
rows().value: Affect was more varied than at intake; worry was evident when discussing employment.

rows().subject: FIN:O-b88833c1
rows().value: Rowan reported completing several small activities since the prior individual appointment, including opening a work message and taking two short walks.

rows().subject: FIN:O-ebd36734
rows().value: Session focused on identifying the prediction behind the delayed reply and separating a brief acknowledgment from a commitment to a specific work schedule; a short response was drafted in Rowan's own words and practiced aloud.

rows().subject: FIN:O-06d9fc53
rows().value: Mara Voss, LCSW noted some improvement in depressive symptoms; ongoing avoidance of work communication and inconsistent sleep. Continue current therapeutic focus and review practical functioning at the next direct appointment.

rows().subject: FIN:O-6c8156d9
rows().value: Mornings remain difficult for Rowan; Rowan becomes quiet when conversation turns to work, as described by Casey.

rows().subject: FIN:O-18ea4787
rows().value: Mara Voss, LCSW noted some improvement in depressive symptoms; ongoing avoidance of work communication and inconsistent sleep.

rows().subject: FIN:O-c14c5ce3
rows().value: Persistent avoidance, difficulty initiating work communication, and sleep disruption remain clinically relevant

rows().subject: FIN:O-75efc40e
rows().value: Patient reported that thinking about work continued to make them want to put things off

rows().subject: FIN:O-5326b379
rows().value: Patient described feeling overwhelmed when other group members discussed workplace demands and worried that returning to work would expose difficulties keeping up.

rows().subject: FIN:O-937fe609
rows().value: When discussion turned to returning to the workplace, Rowan became visibly tense and said the amount of discussion felt difficult to manage.

rows().subject: FIN:O-37a6b31a
rows().value: Work-related task was narrowed to drafting two sentences to a supervisor, without requiring the message be sent today; discussed allowing an incomplete draft to exist rather than abandoning the task because wording felt imperfect.

rows().subject: FIN:O-566aa628
rows().value: Plan: Coordinate with the individual clinician regarding the group experience so that future attendance can be supported without assuming that participation in a group exercise reflects completion of the patient's own work task.

rows().subject: FIN:O-787fcdd4
rows().value: Today's group addressed recognizing the sequence between a triggering situation, an anxious prediction, physical activation, and an avoidance response, using a worked example involving an unanswered work email.

rows().subject: FIN:O-030db061
rows().value: Persistent avoidance and disrupted sleep continue to interfere with resuming a usual work routine.

rows().subject: FIN:O-f16d45cd
rows().value: Rowan was present for the opening check-in and identified anxiety about reconnecting with work.

rows().subject: FIN:O-f4f29c93
rows().value: Rowan reported drafting a short message about a possible gradual return to work but stopping before sending it.

rows().subject: FIN:O-873e934f
rows().value: Rowan used opening a work calendar as an example and described concern that seeing outstanding items would become overwhelming.

rows().subject: FIN:O-c2a161ff
rows().value: Facilitator encouraged a limited, planned review period and a stopping point in response to Rowan's concern about the work calendar.

rows().subject: FIN:O-acc6bbed
rows().value: The outside social worker will provide relevant contact information and offer assistance organizing documents if the patient requests it.

rows().subject: HG-E114
value: Mira Patel, LCSW, and Daniel Shaw, outside social worker

rows().subject: FIN:O-5c2ab9bd
rows().value: The outside social worker reported that Rowan had asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return schedule.

rows().subject: FIN:O-ac172885
rows().value: Coordination of practical supports related to returning to work was discussed between professionals, using the patient's existing release on file.

rows().subject: FIN:O-18c2593c
rows().value: The difference between clinical treatment appointments and the social worker's assistance with gathering employer forms was clarified; neither participant made an employment determination during the call.

rows().subject: FIN:O-33009173
rows().value: Clinician supported a grounding exercise using contact with the chair and feet on the floor, then helped the patient return to the planned wording.

rows().subject: FIN:O-54bd774b
rows().value: Clinical presentation remained consistent with ongoing anxiety, low mood, and functional difficulty around work demands.

rows().subject: FIN:O-07fc9b63
rows().value: Sleep remained uneven, with difficulty settling on nights when work-related thoughts became repetitive.

rows().subject: FIN:O-060f264d
rows().value: Nora Ellis participated directly in the clinical work and helped rehearse a grounding cue for Rowan to use before sending the response.

rows().subject: FIN:O-a2ee9a57
rows().value: Discussed maintaining scheduled treatment contact during the return-to-work planning period and bringing the response draft to the next visit if the patient remained stuck.

rows().subject: FIN:O-cf303024
rows().value: Rowan was able to return to the main request with prompting during role-play.

rows().subject: FIN:O-5e2a1ec0
rows().value: Plan to continue work on avoidance and the bedtime routine.

rows().subject: FIN:O-c66968a7
rows().value: Plan is to continue individual and group work under the existing outpatient plan.

rows().subject: FIN:O-97c1b813
rows().value: Patient anticipated becoming overwhelmed if several work issues were raised at once.

rows().subject: FIN:O-94bf65c3
rows().value: Rowan reported opening the work calendar but delaying a follow-up conversation.

rows().subject: FIN:O-12a3e0eb
rows().value: Rowan remained anxious about the work conversation but could explain the intended first step.

rows().subject: FIN:O-ad8eecd7
rows().value: Rowan shows partial improvement, with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work.

rows().subject: FIN:O-58071af3
rows().value: Continued treatment is appropriate given remaining difficulties with follow-through and work-related functioning.

rows().subject: FIN:O-f63c226f
rows().value: Mood felt less persistently low than earlier in the month, although anxiety remained noticeable when anticipating contact with work.

rows().subject: FIN:O-88a6c6bb
rows().value: Rowan and Casey identified a recurring pattern in which a reminder about contacting work led to a lengthy discussion, followed by Rowan withdrawing from the task.

results.purpose: Find facts about return to work, employment status, or work clearance
results.population: All facts in the episode period with fields or values related to work, employment, or return

passages.text: With the patient's existing release on file, discussed coordination of practical supports related to returning to work. The outside social worker reported that Rowan had asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return schedule. We clarified the difference between the clinical treatment appointments and the social worker's assistance with gathering employer forms. Neither participant made an employment determination during this call.

11:12: Reception notified the clinician that Rowan had not checked in. There was no arrival call or cancellation message on the scheduling line. The appointment remained on the room schedule until its end time.

Reason for care: Rowan describes several weeks of low mood, reduced interest in usual activities, fragmented sleep, and difficulty beginning ordinary tasks. Worry increases when thinking about returning to work after a recent leave. Rowan has been postponing email replies, avoiding conversations about the return date, and spending more time alone at home. They want a routine that makes the work transition feel manageable. The current outpatient episode is planned for January 5 through January 30, with review as treatment progresses.
Review: assess participation, symptoms, and practical functioning during the episode. Adjust the schedule when clinically indicated or when access barriers arise.

Goal 3: support a workable return to employment. Individual sessions will address avoided communication and gradual preparation. Family sessions may address how Rowan can request help and how the partner can offer support without taking over tasks.

The session focused on identifying the prediction behind the delayed reply and separating a brief acknowledgment from a commitment to a specific work schedule. We drafted a short response in Rowan's own words and practiced reading it aloud. Rowan noticed physical tension during the rehearsal but was able to remain with the task. They said the message seemed less overwhelming when it did not need to solve the entire return-to-work question.

We reviewed the activity record and explored the missed appointment from the prior week without treating it as a reason to abandon the schedule. Rowan identified setting out appointment information the evening before as a helpful preparation step. Affect was more varied than at intake, although worry was evident when discussing employment.

Rowan was quiet initially and responded when invited to identify a situation involving avoidance. They described delaying a reply to a work message because they feared being asked for a firm return date. Rowan practiced a breathing exercise and selected reading the message before deciding how to respond as a possible next step. Their participation was relevant to the topic, and they appeared receptive to peer suggestions. The patient attendance roster is maintained by the group desk.

statements.text: The record does not document a date on which Rowan returned to work. Throughout the episode (January 5–30, 2026), Rowan had not yet returned; notes consistently describe ongoing avoidance of work communication, anxiety about reconnecting with work, and persistent functional difficulty around work demands.

No work schedule or employment clearance was approved by the end of the episode. As of January 23, an outside social worker reported that Rowan had asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return schedule, and the professionals clarified that neither of them made an employment determination during that call. The end-of-episode clinician review on January 30 noted partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work, and recommended continued treatment.

statements.why: The evidence comprehensively documents that Rowan had not returned to work during the episode. Multiple findings from across the episode (January 5–30, 2026) consistently show: (1) on 2026-01-05, Rowan reported worry about returning to work, postponing emails, and avoiding conversations about the return date; (2) on 2026-01-19, persistent avoidance and disrupted sleep continued to interfere with resuming work; (3) on 2026-01-30, partial improvement was noted but with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work, and anxiety remained when anticipating contact with work. The statement that 'the record does not document a date on which Rowan returned to work' is supported by the absence of any finding indicating an actual return and the consistent documentation of ongoing avoidance, anxiety, and functional difficulty throughout the episode.

The evidence clearly supports that no work schedule or employment clearance was approved by the end of the episode. The January 23 encounter documents that Rowan asked for help understanding whom to contact about a gradual return schedule, but the clinician explicitly clarified that 'neither participant made an employment determination during this call.' The end-of-episode clinician review on January 30 noted partial improvement with persistent avoidance and meaningful functional impact around returning to work, and recommended continued treatment—with no mention of any approved schedule or clearance. The evidence directly supports the statement that no such approval occurred.

question: Can the documents establish whether psychotherapy or medication caused the PHQ-9 improvement, or which treatment was more effective?

statements.text: The documents cannot establish whether psychotherapy or medication caused the PHQ-9 improvement, nor which treatment was more effective. No clinician formulation, attribution statement, or comparative effectiveness claim appears anywhere in the record.

The closest any clinician came to linking the score change to a treatment was a January 16 note stating that 'the score and recent individual-session material suggest some improvement in depressive symptoms' — a tentative observation tying the PHQ-9 result to therapy content, not a causal attribution. No note credits medication, and no note compares the two modalities.

Both treatments were running concurrently throughout the period: psychotherapy (individual, group, and family sessions) was the primary documented modality, while medication management visits explicitly noted that no psychotherapy was provided at those encounters and that psychotherapy goals remained with the treating therapist. The record contains no controlled comparison, no washout period, and no clinician statement attributing the score change to either treatment alone or to their combination. Attribution or comparative effectiveness cannot be determined from these documents.

omitted.text: The PHQ-9 total score fell from 18 on January 5 to 10 on January 30, a drop of 8 points (44.4%).

queries.purpose: Retrieve all PHQ-9 total scores to compute the score change over the review period
queries.population: All PHQ-9 total scores (item = none) recorded during the review period
queries.query: from measurements where instrument = 'PHQ-9' and item = none and date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 select list(date, score, status, sources) change(score) percent_change(score)

queries.purpose: Retrieve clinician findings that explicitly discuss attribution of improvement, comparative effectiveness, medication effect, psychotherapy effect, or formulation linking treatment to PHQ-9 change
queries.population: All clinician-reported findings of any type that mention medication, psychotherapy, PHQ-9, attribution, or treatment response
queries.query: from findings where reporter = clinician and date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 and (text contains 'PHQ' or text contains 'medic' or text contains 'psychotherapy' or text contains 'attribut' or text contains 'caused' or text contains 'effective' or text contains 'improvement' or text contains 'formul') select rows()

queries.purpose: Retrieve response and intervention findings from any reporter that may link treatment modality to symptom change
queries.population: All findings typed as response, intervention, or plan recorded during the review period
queries.query: from findings where date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 and type in (response, intervention, plan) select rows()

queries.purpose: Retrieve the medication record to establish what medication was active and when, for timeline comparison with PHQ-9 scores
queries.population: All medication records in the review period
queries.query: from medications where date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 select rows()

queries.purpose: Retrieve any facts or open items that document a clinician formulation, attribution statement, or conflict about treatment effectiveness or PHQ-9 causation
queries.population: All facts and open items related to treatment attribution, formulation, or PHQ-9 interpretation
queries.query: from facts where date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 and (field contains 'attribut' or field contains 'formul' or field contains 'PHQ' or field contains 'medic' or field contains 'psychotherapy' or field contains 'effective' or value contains 'attribut' or value contains 'formul' or value contains 'PHQ' or value contains 'caused') select rows()

checklist: The magnitude of PHQ-9 score change over the review period
Whether any clinician formulation explicitly links the score change to psychotherapy, medication, or both
Whether the documents contain any comparative effectiveness statement or attribution of improvement to one treatment over the other
Whether the record contains sufficient documentation to settle attribution or comparative effectiveness, or whether that determination is beyond what the documents establish
plan.reason: The record contains PHQ-9 scores, medication data, and therapy attendance, but whether a clinician formulation explicitly attributing the score change to one or both treatments exists is uncertain from the catalogue alone. Queries 2, 3, and 5 will reveal whether such a formulation is documented; if none is found, the attribution question cannot be settled from the record.

required_totals.item: PHQ-9 score change over the review period

results.query: from measurements where instrument = 'PHQ-9' and item = none and date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 select list(date, score, status, sources) change(score) percent_change(score)
results.purpose: Retrieve all PHQ-9 total scores to compute the score change over the review period
results.population: All PHQ-9 total scores (item = none) recorded during the review period

results.query: from findings where reporter = clinician and date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 and (text contains 'PHQ' or text contains 'medic' or text contains 'psychotherapy' or text contains 'attribut' or text contains 'caused' or text contains 'effective' or text contains 'improvement' or text contains 'formul') select rows()
