results.query: from findings where date >= 2026-01-05 and date <= 2026-01-30 and type in (response, intervention, plan) select rows()

rows().text: Goal 3: individual sessions will address avoided communication and gradual preparation to support a workable return to employment; family sessions may address how Rowan can request help and how the partner can offer support without taking over tasks.

Plan: participate in scheduled individual, group, and selected family appointments; bring the activity record to the next individual appointment; treatment goals and proposed weekly schedule to be recorded in a separate plan.
The treatment team will combine individual practice, therapeutic group activities, and family work when Rowan is present.

Rowan selected opening their work inbox for five minutes without requiring an immediate reply as a behavioral step; discussed setting a consistent morning anchor and recording the time they get out of bed.

Goal 2: Rowan will practice one grounding or paced-breathing exercise and establish a consistent morning routine to improve coping with anxiety and disrupted sleep; group participation will provide opportunities to rehearse skills and hear alternative approaches.

Goal 1: Rowan will select manageable activities, track attempts, and review barriers with the individual therapist to improve daily activity and task initiation; emphasis on completion of useful steps rather than judging the day by mood alone.
Rowan wants a routine that makes the work transition feel manageable.
Plan to assess participation, symptoms, and practical functioning during the episode; adjust the schedule when clinically indicated or when access barriers arise.

Interventions included: developing a shared description of the sleep, worry, and avoidance cycle; introducing behavioral activation; and practicing breaking one work-related task into a short, observable step.
Rowan practiced a breathing exercise and selected reading the message before deciding how to respond as a possible next step.
Following the break, the facilitator resumed with a paired planning exercise and a group discussion of barriers to practice at home.

Group focus was recognizing early physical signs of anxiety and choosing a coping response before withdrawing from a task; members used recent everyday situations to describe the relationship between thoughts, body sensations, and behavior.
Rowan's participation was relevant to the topic and they appeared receptive to peer suggestions.
The facilitator demonstrated paced breathing, invited short practice rounds, and led discussion about using a skill during a manageable task rather than only after distress has peaked.
No therapy intervention was conducted during the callback; the individual clinician was notified of the missed appointment so that barriers to attendance could be discussed at the next visit.

Patient confirmed they still intended to attend the next day's family visit with Casey; staff verified appointment time and location and offered to resend the existing appointment list; patient requested the list through the portal.
Following HG-E103 no-show, outreach was assigned to the individual therapist's support queue.
Rowan agreed to say when they wanted practical assistance versus quiet company.
Rowan said the evening walk felt more acceptable than a lengthy review of unfinished tasks.

Clinicians mapped a recent morning interaction, pausing at points where each person made assumptions; Rowan practiced asking for one specific kind of help and Casey practiced reflecting the request before offering suggestions.
The agreed home practice and ongoing treatment plan are recorded in Mara Voss's primary note for HG-E104.
Casey agreed to use a single planned check-in about work preparation instead of repeated reminders.
Leena Park guided a short communication rehearsal while Mara Voss observed and helped the pair identify language they could use during the next week.
Casey reflected Rowan's wish to keep ownership of the return-to-work process.
The couple selected an evening walk as a shared activity without making it a discussion about progress.
Rowan remained present and engaged throughout the visit and became more animated when describing a shared evening walk, identifying it as support that did not feel like pressure.
Plan: try the planned check-in and review its effect at the next individual visit; continue the small activity steps selected in treatment.
Both Rowan and Casey were able to acknowledge that their intentions differed from how the other person experienced the exchange.
Clinician asked each participant to reflect the other person's concern before moving to a solution; both participants completed the reflective listening exercise.
Session focused on patterns of support at home as Rowan attempts to rebuild a routine.
The rehearsal became less defensive with repetition; both participants contributed ideas for a brief, predictable check-in.
Rowan was able to state that Casey wanted reassurance that some preparation was happening.
Members reviewed how postponement can briefly reduce discomfort while making the next attempt feel harder.
The facilitator reinforced restarting with a smaller step and reviewing what interfered when an attempt is missed.
The group closed with members naming their next practice attempt. Attendance is recorded on the group desk roster.

The second portion of the group included creating an activity ladder, anticipating obstacles, and rehearsing a neutral response to a missed attempt. Members were encouraged to specify the next action in concrete terms, including when and where it could take place.
During the planning exercise, Rowan wrote down an action to try after breakfast and asked how to respond if the morning went poorly.
Today's group addressed behavioral activation and the difference between an activity being possible and it feeling easy.
Rowan described taking a walk with Casey over the weekend and noted that it helped the evening feel less dominated by worry.
Medication monitoring will continue during the outpatient episode, with later follow-up arranged according to clinical response.
Rowan was attentive, asked questions about the monitoring plan, and could restate the next steps.
Rowan is engaged with the therapy program and intends to continue the scheduled appointments.
Clinician discussed practical adherence supports, the expected follow-up process, and when to contact the prescribing office about changes in symptoms or tolerability.
The medication list was reviewed with Rowan and reconciled with the active chart.
No separate psychotherapy component was provided or documented. Rowan was directed to bring activity and communication concerns to the treating therapist for continued work.

Rowan noticed physical tension during the rehearsal but was able to remain with the task; they said the message seemed less overwhelming when it did not need to solve the entire return-to-work question.
Plan includes maintaining planned group participation and family involvement as available.
Rowan described the family appointment as helpful because the planned check-in with Casey reduced repeated reminders.
Plan: attempt the drafted acknowledgment, continue morning activity tracking, and practice the breathing skill before an avoided task; Rowan will review the result at the next individual visit.

Session focused on identifying the prediction behind the delayed reply and separating a brief acknowledgment from a commitment to a specific work schedule; a short response was drafted in Rowan's own words and practiced aloud.
The activity record was reviewed and the missed appointment from the prior week was explored without treating it as a reason to abandon the schedule.
Portal notice stated that the office initiated the cancellation and that the participant should not come to the group room.
A cancellation message was released to all registered members following HG-E108 clinic cancellation due to staff illness.
Registered participants were contacted before the planned group start time to notify them of the cancellation.

results.purpose: Retrieve any facts or open items that document a clinician formulation, attribution statement, or conflict about treatment effectiveness or PHQ-9 causation
results.population: All facts and open items related to treatment attribution, formulation, or PHQ-9 interpretation

passages.text: Both participants agreed to try one brief check-in at a planned time rather than repeated questions across the evening. Rowan remained anxious about the work conversation but could explain the intended first step. The patient reported that having a limited plan felt more manageable. Continue the current outpatient treatment plan and revisit whether the agreed communication pattern was useful.

The service consisted of medication evaluation and management, including symptom review and medication counseling. No separately documented psychotherapy was provided. Ongoing psychotherapy goals and behavioral assignments remain with the treating therapist. Rowan agreed to continue attending scheduled outpatient follow-up and to bring questions about the medication regimen to the next medication appointment.

Local treatment participation goal: at least 3 therapy days and at least 150 minutes of patient-present therapy in each Monday–Sunday week. A therapy day is a calendar day on which Rowan participates in individual, group, or family psychotherapy. Patient-present individual, group, and family therapy contribute to the minute goal. Medication management, contacts with collateral informants only, and care coordination do not contribute. This is the program's individualized treatment-plan goal for Rowan.

Service documented: medication review and management only. No separate psychotherapy component was provided or documented. Rowan was directed to bring activity and communication concerns to the treating therapist for continued work.

The couple selected an evening walk as an activity they could share without making it a discussion about progress. Rowan said this felt more acceptable than a lengthy review of unfinished tasks. The agreed home practice and ongoing treatment plan are recorded in Mara Voss's primary note for HG-E104.

Goal 2: improve coping with anxiety and disrupted sleep. Rowan will practice one grounding or paced-breathing exercise and establish a consistent morning routine. Group participation will provide opportunities to rehearse skills and hear alternative approaches.

Rowan did not join in person, by telephone, or by video. No patient-present psychotherapy occurred during this contact. Information from Casey will be incorporated into the next direct clinical review with Rowan. No new treatment decision was made with Rowan during this appointment.

statements.text: The documents cannot establish whether psychotherapy or medication caused the PHQ-9 improvement, nor which treatment was more effective. No clinician formulation, attribution statement, or comparative effectiveness claim appears anywhere in the record.
The PHQ-9 total score fell from 18 on January 5 to 10 on January 30, a drop of 8 points (44.4%).

The closest any clinician came to linking the score change to a treatment was a January 16 note stating that 'the score and recent individual-session material suggest some improvement in depressive symptoms' — a tentative observation tying the PHQ-9 result to therapy content, not a causal attribution. No note credits medication, and no note compares the two modalities.

Both treatments were running concurrently throughout the period: psychotherapy (individual, group, and family sessions) was the primary documented modality, while medication management visits explicitly noted that no psychotherapy was provided at those encounters and that psychotherapy goals remained with the treating therapist. The record contains no controlled comparison, no washout period, and no clinician statement attributing the score change to either treatment alone or to their combination. Attribution or comparative effectiveness cannot be determined from these documents.

question_parts.part: Can the documents establish whether psychotherapy caused the PHQ-9 improvement?
Can the documents establish whether medication caused the PHQ-9 improvement?
Can the documents establish which treatment was more effective?

checklist.item: The magnitude of PHQ-9 score change over the review period
Whether any clinician formulation explicitly links the score change to psychotherapy, medication, or both
Whether the documents contain any comparative effectiveness statement or attribution of improvement to one treatment over the other
Whether the record contains sufficient documentation to settle attribution or comparative effectiveness, or whether that determination is beyond what the documents establish

statements.why: The evidence from R2 (clinician findings) comprehensively documents the absence of any attribution statement, causal claim, or comparative effectiveness statement. The cited passages show that clinicians noted 'some improvement in depressive symptoms' (FIN:O-acbce97e, FIN:O-18ea4787) and 'partial improvement' (FIN:O-ad8eecd7), but made no causal attribution to either treatment. The only tentative link is FIN:O-acbce97e stating that 'the score and recent individual-session material suggest some improvement,' which is a suggestive observation, not a causal attribution. No passage credits medication alone, and no passage compares the two modalities. The statement is fully supported.

The evidence from R1 directly documents the PHQ-9 score change: baseline score of 18.0 on 2026-01-05, final score of 10.0 on 2026-01-30, with a change of -8.0 points and a percent change of -44.4%. The fact values quote the source documents: 'total score 18' and 'PHQ-9 total: 10.' The magnitude is concretely established.

The evidence demonstrates that the closest any clinician came to linking the score change to treatment was FIN:O-acbce97e on 2026-01-16, which states 'Clinician notes the score and recent individual-session material suggest some improvement in depressive symptoms.' This is a tentative observation ('suggest') that ties the PHQ-9 result to therapy content (individual-session material), not a definitive causal attribution. The word 'suggest' indicates inference rather than established causation. No note credits medication, and no note compares the two modalities. The statement is supported by the cited evidence.

The evidence from R2, R3, and R4 establishes that both treatments ran concurrently: psychotherapy (individual, group, family sessions documented in R3) and medication management (R4 shows medication records throughout the period). The cited passages show that medication management visits explicitly noted 'No separately documented psychotherapy was provided' (FIN:O-8b159802, FIN:O-f7accf3e), and that 'Ongoing psychotherapy goals and behavioral assignments remain with the treating therapist' (FIN:O-7d815a86). The record contains no controlled comparison, no washout period, and no clinician statement attributing the score change to either treatment alone or to their combination. The statement that attribution or comparative effectiveness cannot be determined is fully supported by the absence of such documentation.

populations.why: R1 queries 'from measurements where instrument = 'PHQ-9' and item = none' for the review period 2026-01-05 to 2026-01-30. The population is all PHQ-9 total scores (item = none) recorded during the review period. This matches the question's request for PHQ-9 score change over the review period. The result correctly identifies the baseline (18.0 on 2026-01-05) and final (10.0 on 2026-01-30) scores.

R2 queries clinician-reported findings that mention PHQ, medication, psychotherapy, attribution, causation, effectiveness, improvement, or formulation during the review period. This population matches the question's need to identify whether any clinician formulation explicitly links the score change to treatment. The result correctly returns all relevant clinician findings, including those that note improvement without attribution (FIN:O-acbce97e, FIN:O-18ea4787, FIN:O-ad8eecd7) and those that document treatment modalities (FIN:O-8b159802, FIN:O-f7accf3e, FIN:O-7d815a86).

R3 queries findings typed as response, intervention, or plan during the review period. This population captures the full range of clinical documentation that could contain attribution or comparative effectiveness statements. The result correctly identifies treatment-related findings across the episode.

R4 queries all medication records during the review period. This population is appropriate for establishing that medication management was occurring concurrently with psychotherapy, which is necessary context for evaluating whether attribution or comparative effectiveness can be determined.

R5 queries facts and open items related to treatment attribution, formulation, PHQ-9 interpretation, medication, psychotherapy, or effectiveness during the review period. This population is appropriate for identifying any structured data or open items that might document attribution or comparative effectiveness claims.

question: Identify the documented clinicians for January 9 family therapy, January 19 therapy, January 26 individual therapy, and January 30 medication management. Do multiple clinicians imply additional patient sessions?

statements.text: January 9 family therapy: two clinicians are documented — Mara Voss, LCSW (primary) and Leena Park, LPC (co-facilitator). January 19 therapy: the skills group was facilitated by Leah Chen, LCSW; the same-day individual session was conducted by Mira Patel, LCSW — these are two separate encounters, each with one clinician. January 26 individual therapy: two clinicians are documented — Mira Patel, LCSW and Nora Ellis, LCSW, both present in the same session. January 30 medication management: one clinician is documented — Elena Ortiz, PMHNP.

Multiple clinicians on a single date do not imply additional patient sessions. On January 9, Mara Voss and Leena Park co-facilitated one 45-minute family session together. On January 26, Mira Patel and Nora Ellis both participated in one individual session; Nora Ellis's note is a participating-clinician record filed under the same encounter. On January 19, the two clinicians (Leah Chen and Mira Patel) each led a distinct, separately documented encounter — the individual session was added because Rowan became anxious during group and came directly from the group room, not because a second clinician was present.

passages.text:
To: Outpatient program authorization desk
The requested group service authorization is approved for the period January 5, 2026 through January 30, 2026. Authorized quantity: 8 group sessions. One authorization unit represents one scheduled group session. The service description is outpatient therapeutic group work supporting the submitted behavioral health treatment plan. This letter does not authorize individual therapy, family therapy, or medication appointments under the group service quantity.

Local treatment participation goal: at least 3 therapy days and at least 150 minutes of patient-present therapy in each Monday–Sunday week. A therapy day is a calendar day on which Rowan participates in individual, group, or family psychotherapy. Patient-present individual, group, and family therapy contribute to the minute goal. Medication management, contacts with collateral informants only, and care coordination do not contribute. This is the program's individualized treatment-plan goal for Rowan.

Records intake: indexed by Ana Reed, records assistant, January 26, 2026, 16:31. This is a retransmission of the January 19 roster for HG-E110. The received copy contains no new clinician signature and records no additional visit.

Goal 3: support a workable return to employment. Individual sessions will address avoided communication and gradual preparation. Family sessions may address how Rowan can request help and how the partner can offer support without taking over tasks.

statements.text: Yes, the early-January and later-January records refer to the same patient, Rowan Mercer. Despite a change in individual clinicians (Mara Voss, LCSW in early January through January 16; Mira Patel, LCSW from January 19 onward) and group facilitators (Leena Park, LPC early; Leah Chen, LCSW later), all encounters share the same patient name, the same partner (Casey Mercer), and a continuous clinical narrative about the same presenting problems.

The chart identifiers supporting the match are: (1) the shared encounter ID series HG-E101 through HG-E120, all filed under the same outpatient chart; (2) document BH-D006 (the appointment desk export), which appears as a source record for every early-January encounter (HG-E101 through HG-E109) and links them to the same chart; (3) the January 19 group attendance record explicitly states 'the patient retained the same outpatient chart identifier throughout the day's services,' bridging the early- and later-January periods; and (4) the patient name Rowan Mercer and partner Casey Mercer appear consistently across all documents on both sides of the clinician transition.

question: What reasons are documented for Rowan’s partial group attendance on January 6 and late arrival on January 22? Can the same explanation be assigned to both dates?

statements.text: On January 6, the record documents two reasons for partial attendance: Rowan arrived late after difficulty finding parking (calling from the building entrance to say they were running behind), and left early for a previously arranged ride.

On January 22, the record documents only "late arrival" as the reason for partial attendance. Rowan arrived at 10:30 and remained until the group closed at 11:30; no reason for the late arrival is recorded.

The same explanation cannot be assigned to both dates. On January 6, parking difficulty is explicitly documented as the cause of late arrival, and an early departure for a pre-arranged ride also contributed to the partial attendance. On January 22, no cause for the late arrival is recorded — the record notes only that Rowan joined after the group had begun. A note documenting the reason for the January 22 late arrival would be needed to determine whether the circumstances were the same.

question: Would the appointment-status export alone support an accurate therapy-minute total for January 5–16? Identify what additional evidence is necessary.

statements.text: The appointment-status export alone is not sufficient to produce an accurate therapy-minute total for January 5–16. It confirms which appointments were attended or missed, but it does not record the actual minutes of patient-present therapy for each session — those figures come from session notes, time logs, and attendance rosters, not from the export itself.

To verify that 260-minute total, the following additional evidence beyond the appointment-status export is necessary: (1) session notes or time logs for each attended encounter to establish actual patient-present start and end times (the export records no clock times for the patient's presence); (2) the group attendance roster for HG-E102 and HG-E105, which document arrival/departure times and break intervals used to compute creditable minutes; (3) the clinical notes for HG-E104 (family) confirming both participants were present for the full 45 minutes; and (4) confirmation that no charges or billing records exist for the period that would indicate additional encounters not captured in the export — the record contains no charges for January 5–16.

Four encounters in the period cannot be confirmed as creditable therapy minutes from appointment-status alone: HG-E103 (January 8, individual — no-show, patient did not attend, excluded); HG-E108 (January 15, group — cancelled by the clinic due to staff illness, no session held, excluded); HG-E109 (January 16, collateral — patient was absent for the entire contact, excluded); and HG-E102 (January 6, group — appointment-status shows only 'partial,' which does not itself establish how many minutes the patient was present; the 45 creditable minutes come from the session note and attendance roster recording arrival at 10:15, departure at 11:15, and a break from 10:45 to 11:00).

The verified therapy-minute total for January 5–16, covering the five goal-eligible (individual, group, and family) encounters in which the patient was present — HG-E101 (50 min), HG-E102 (45 min), HG-E104 (45 min), HG-E105 (75 min), and HG-E107 (45 min) — is 260 minutes.

statements.text: The appointment-status export alone is not sufficient to produce an accurate therapy-minute total for January 5–16. It confirms which appointments were attended or missed, but it does not record the actual minutes of patient-present therapy for each session — those figures come from session notes, time logs, and attendance rosters, not from the export itself.

Four encounters in the period cannot be confirmed as creditable therapy minutes from appointment-status alone: HG-E103 (January 8, individual — no-show, patient did not attend, excluded); HG-E108 (January 15, group — cancelled by the clinic due to staff illness, no session held, excluded); HG-E109 (January 16, collateral — patient was absent for the entire contact, excluded); and HG-E102 (January 6, group — appointment-status shows only 'partial,' which does not itself establish how many minutes the patient was present; the 45 creditable minutes come from the session note and attendance roster recording arrival at 10:15, departure at 11:15, and a break from 10:45 to 11:00).

The verified therapy-minute total for January 5–16, covering the five goal-eligible (individual, group, and family) encounters in which the patient was present — HG-E101 (50 min), HG-E102 (45 min), HG-E104 (45 min), HG-E105 (75 min), and HG-E107 (45 min) — is 260 minutes.

To verify that 260-minute total, the following additional evidence beyond the appointment-status export is necessary: (1) session notes or time logs for each attended encounter to establish actual patient-present start and end times (the export records no clock times for the patient's presence); (2) the group attendance roster for HG-E102 and HG-E105, which document arrival/departure times and break intervals used to compute creditable minutes; (3) the clinical notes for HG-E104 (family) confirming both participants were present for the full 45 minutes; and (4) confirmation that no charges or billing records exist for the period that would indicate additional encounters not captured in the export — the record contains no charges for January 5–16.

The evidence demonstrates that the export alone cannot establish the actual minutes of patient-present therapy—those figures require session notes, time logs, and attendance rosters. For example, HG-E102 shows 'partial' status in the export, but the actual 45 creditable minutes are derived from arrival/departure times (10:15–11:15 with a 10:45–11:00 break) documented in session notes and the attendance roster, not from the export itself.

The statement correctly identifies four encounters that cannot be confirmed as creditable from appointment-status alone: HG-E103 (no-show, disposition excluded), HG-E108 (cancelled by clinic, disposition excluded), HG-E109 (patient absent, disposition excluded), and HG-E102 (partial status, requiring session notes and roster to establish the 45 creditable minutes). R1.1 confirms the attendance and disposition values for each; the facts confirm HG-E103, HG-E108, and HG-E109 are excluded; and the facts for HG-E102 show the 45-minute calculation derives from documented arrival/departure times and break intervals, not from the export's 'partial' status alone.

The statement is directly supported by R2.1, which sums the minutes for the five goal-eligible encounters (HG-E101, HG-E102, HG-E104, HG-E105, HG-E107) to 260 minutes. The individual minute values are confirmed by facts: HG-E101 = 50 min, HG-E102 = 45 min, HG-E104 = 45 min, HG-E105 = 75 min, HG-E107 = 45 min. All five encounters have disposition = included and were delivered (patient present).

The statement is supported by the evidence showing that session notes, time logs, and attendance rosters are necessary to establish actual patient-present times (R1.1 documents show these sources for each encounter); R2.1 confirms the 260-minute total; facts for HG-E102 and HG-E105 show arrival/departure times and break intervals used to compute creditable minutes; facts for HG-E104 confirm both participants were present for the full 45 minutes; and R5.1 (charges query) returns no results, confirming no charges exist for January 5–16 that would indicate additional encounters.

question: What targeted clarification would settle the unresolved January 26 time and the resulting final-week goal status? Which already available administrative records would not resolve it?

statements.text: The conflict would be settled by asking one of the two clinicians who signed the January 26 individual psychotherapy note — Mira Patel, LCSW (primary record, signed 11:16) or Nora Ellis, LCSW (second record, signed 12:03) — to confirm the actual session start time: 09:00 (as the primary record states, giving 50 minutes) or 09:10 (as the second record states, giving 40 minutes). Both documents are final and of equal standing, so a direct attestation or a contemporaneous time-stamp (e.g., an EHR login log or room-entry record) from either clinician would resolve which start time is correct.

Resolving the start time would determine whether the January 26 session contributes 50 minutes (09:00 start) or 40 minutes (09:10 start) to the final week. The other two included visits that week contribute a fixed 75 minutes (January 29 group) and 30 minutes (January 30 family), totalling either 155 or 145 minutes against the 150-minute threshold. At 50 minutes the week total is 155 minutes — threshold met. At 40 minutes the total is 145 minutes — threshold not met. The 3-therapy-days threshold is met under either scenario (3 distinct days attended). Overall goal status is therefore met if the start time is 09:00, and not met if it is 09:10; it cannot be determined until the conflict is resolved. This is a partial week (Monday–Friday only).

The two already-available administrative records — the appointment desk export and the early appointment status export — would not resolve the conflict. Both record the appointment as attended and show the scheduled slot, but neither captures the actual patient-contact start time; they cannot distinguish between 09:00 and 09:10. Similarly, the two final clinical notes (BH-D110 and BH-D111) are the very sources that disagree, so they cannot settle each other.
